On November 12, 2026, Columbia Business School researcher Hannah Li released a theoretical and empirical study analyzing how endogenous human adaptation undermines standard evaluation methods for interactive large language model (LLM) systems. The preprint, titled [When Both Sides Adapt: The Challenges of Evaluating Interactive LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17239) (arXiv:2611.17239v1), demonstrates that as human users observe model outputs, they alter prompting strategies and task difficulty, systematically distorting offline benchmarks and live A/B testing comparisons. ## Two Divergent Estimands: Common Versus Induced Distributions Modern machine learning teams evaluate generative models through two primary methods: offline benchmark testing on static datasets and live A/B testing on randomized user cohorts. Li proves that these approaches target fundamentally distinct statistical quantities in interactive systems. Offline benchmarks evaluate candidate models on a fixed prompt distribution, isolating performance differentials on identical tasks. In contrast, live randomized trials evaluate models across prompt distributions dynamically induced by each model. In automated pipelines, evaluators rely on an offline [model evaluation suite](/dictionary/term/model-evaluation-suite) or a static [synthetic benchmark](/dictionary/term/synthetic-benchmark) to calculate what Li terms the common-distribution effect. This estimand fixes the prompt distribution and measures computational differences. However, in live production environments, users observe completions and adapt. A user receiving a high-quality answer escalates to difficult tasks, whereas a user receiving unhelpful output lowers task difficulty, uses rigid templates, or leaves. Consequently, difference-in-means estimators in live A/B trials converge to an induced-distribution effect, which conflates model capability with endogenous shifts in task difficulty. ## The Mechanics of Ranking Reversals The study formally demonstrates that these differing estimands cause ranking reversals, where Model A outperforms Model B on every prompt category, yet Model B achieves higher aggregate satisfaction in live trials. On November 14, 2026, researchers from Stanford University’s SNAP group, in collaboration with computer scientists from MIT, the University of Pennsylvania, and the University of Toronto, open-sourced Memorilla, an architecture that provides frozen large language models with persistent, query-conditioned access to extensive document collections. By translating document corpora into compact latent vectors rather than packing raw text into prompts, Memorilla compresses context by over a hundredfold while preserving critical facts and inter-document relationships across long-horizon research and agent workflows. ## Open-Source Release and Core Technical Architecture The Memorilla system, published under the permissive Apache 2.0 license, was developed by doctoral researchers Adibvafa Fallahpour, Parsa Idehpour, Vignesh Kothapalli, Nikita Mounier, Shirley Wu, and Shayan Pardis alongside Professor Jure Leskovec at the Stanford Network Analysis Project (SNAP). The codebase is hosted on GitHub at <https://github.com/snap-stanford/memorilla>, with pre-trained checkpoints on Hugging Face at <https://huggingface.co/memorilla> and interactive documentation at <https://memory.stanford.edu/>. Theoretical foundations and benchmark validations appear in the preprint *Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs* on arXiv ([arXiv:2610.21375](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21375)). Rather than requiring model parameter fine-tuning or expanding active context windows, Memorilla acts as a modular bridge connecting frozen document encoders to frozen text decoders. The framework meets established [open-source model criteria](/dictionary/term/open-source-model-criteria), distributing complete training recipes, attention profiling harnesses, and evaluation suites. It was trained entirely on Chinese hardware and performs at the level US models like Claude Opus 5 reached a few months ago on coding benchmarks.** The LongCat team at Chinese food delivery company Meituan has released the weights for LongCat-2.5, one week after the model's official unveiling. LongCat-2.5 is built for agents that work through long, multi-step tasks autonomously, particularly coding. According to Meituan, it comes close to top Western models on several benchmarks. LongCat-2.5 is a mixture-of-experts model that activates only a subset of its specialized subnetworks for each token it processes. Out of 1.6 trillion total parameters, roughly 48 billion are active per token. Through the API, the model handles up to one million tokens at once and generates responses up to 128,000 tokens long. It understands text, images, and video, responds in text, and lets users toggle reasoning on and off. ## LongCat-2.5 converts images into tokens LongCat-2.5 builds on its [predecessor LongCat-2.0](https://the-decoder.com/meituans-longcat-2-0-shows-china-can-train-massive-ai-models-without-nvidia/) and adds image understanding. Many multimodal models bolt on a separate image encoder after the fact. LongCat-2.5 instead converts images into tokens that the model processes alongside text, as is standard practice for today's LLMs. The approach draws on the research model LongCat-Next and aims to improve visual coding, design, and 3D tasks. [![](https://the-decoder.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/longcat-25-02-visual-tokenization.jpg)](https://the-decoder.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/longcat-25-02-visual-tokenization.jpg) LongCat-2.5 breaks images down at their native resolution into discrete tokens that the model processes alongside text. | Image: Meituan For reinforcement learning, the team used real software tasks from GitHub pull requests along with recreated agent failures. To make sure the model actually solved the tasks during training, the developers blocked internet access in the training environments, removed Git history and cached files, and had a language model check its solutions for tricks. The team also distilled the capabilities of several specialized teacher models for agent work, reasoning, and dialog into LongCat-2.5. highlights.content: [![](https://assets.bizclikmedia.net/original/5401dac120314d7e0f03205da6e95493:6da76f0b8571199734ddc929a0b434ce/technology-magazine-light-logo.png)](/ "Home") Article AI & Machine Learning # Asana’s CPO on why workflow readiness beats AI model hype By[Alice Chambers](/author/alice-chambers) November 15, 2026 undefined mins Share this article **Prioritise Us** on Google Share this article **Prioritise Us** on Google ![](https://assets.bizclikmedia.net/138/791a25a17528cda49d3c3849bd6fbfcd:d906b26b7f217c9f6783576bd3265f53/arnab-bose.webp) “AI can produce useful output and complete individual tasks, but enterprises need more,” Arnab says Arnab Bose, Chief Product Officer at Asana, reveals how StackAI’s integration and shared operating layers help enterprises scale AI agents safely Since joining [Asana](https://technologymagazine.com/company/asana) as Chief Product Officer in September 2025 – following a six-year tenure at Okta – [Arnab Bose](https://technologymagazine.com/executive/arnab-bose) has led the company’s product strategy, focusing on how enterprises coordinate complex work across human and AI teams. In this Q&A, Arnab explores why organisations struggle to move artificial intelligence beyond isolated pilots into scaled, high-impact operations. He discusses closing the human-agent coordination gap, the importance of “workflow readiness”, and how a shared operating layer bolstered by Asana’s acquisition of StackAI – provides essential context, governance and accountability to embed AI directly where enterprise work already happens. ## A year into your role – what’s the problem you’re now more convinced than ever nobody has solved yet? The hardest problem an organisation continues to face isn’t whether an AI agent can perform a certain task, we know it can. Instead, the biggest challenge is closing the coordination gap between humans and agents. AI can produce useful output and complete individual tasks, but enterprises need more. Truly collaborative work involves shared goals, dependencies, decisions, approvals and handoffs, factors often beyond isolated AI agents’ capabilities. To bridge this gap, agents need access to the right context for a task; that context turns AI from generic output into meaningful value. Currently, many AI experiences still operate around one person, one prompt and one agent, essentially operating in a ‘black box’. This single player approach leads to work that lacks crucial context and therefore often misses the mark. According to recent Asana research, only 18% of UK workers say AI agents meet their needs, while 33% say they address some important needs, revealing significant gaps in AI utility. Bridging these gaps and scaling AI to become truly impactful remains a key challenge. For me, the remaining problem is embedding AI agents within existing workflows and giving them a shared system of context, memory and coordination. ## What does the gap between a successful pilot and a scaled workflow actually look like? Pilots are an important starting point, but they are also often where organisations get stuck. Pilots tend to operate in a narrow environment with isolated information and under close human supervision. This often means pilots succeed within their limited parameters and under close human management; the challenge comes when they scale across an organisation, where those strict parameters become huge ecosystems. A scaled workflow, by contrast, has AI agents operating with organisation-wide intelligence informing their work at all times. Pilots often stall at scale because context is lost across applications, tools and software; handoffs become invisible; and ownership becomes unclear. To scale a successful pilot, embed AI where work already happens, rather than treating AI tools as an add-on. A successful pilot may demonstrate that an AI agent can complete a task. On November 12, 2026, researchers from Navers Lab, Einsia.AI, and Tsinghua University released Visual Cipher Bench, a rigorous multimodal benchmark assessing long-horizon visual reasoning in autonomous LLM agents across 40 original puzzle tasks without text guidance. Frontier models achieved an overall accuracy of only 26.7% for the leading configuration, exposing a critical capability gap for academic AI laboratories and evaluation researchers relying on text-centric benchmarks. ## Benchmark Architecture: 40 Multi-Step Puzzles and Withheld Text Hints The research team led by Deyao Hong, Jiayi Jiang, Yuchun Chen, Yixuan Shi, and Huan-ang Gao published their findings in [Visual Cipher Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Visual Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16861) (arXiv:2611.16861). The benchmark codebase and dataset are available on [GitHub](https://github.com/Einsia/Visual-Cipher-Bench) and the [Einsia.AI project platform](https://lab.einsia.ai/visual-cipher-bench/). While frontier language-model agents achieve high performance on coding benchmarks like SWE-bench and SWE-Bench Pro, these evaluations rely on explicit text issue descriptions and immediate compiler or test execution feedback. Visual Cipher Bench evaluates whether long-horizon capabilities transfer to visual domains where critical logic is embedded entirely in images and execution feedback is absent. The benchmark introduces 40 original visual ciphers spanning 67 line drawings, divided into four categories of 10 puzzles each: * **P1: Spatial manipulation and simulation:** Multi-step geometric rotations, trajectory projections, and topological folding. * **P2: Logical constraints and planning:** Combinatorial constraint satisfaction, grid placements, and discrete scheduling. * **P3: Rule induction:** Inferring procedural transformation functions from visual input-output pairs without instructions. * **P4: Knowledge-based decoding:** Multi-layered ciphers connecting visual glyphs to lexical, numeric, or semantic patterns. Microsoft Azure provides services and development frameworks that can support the construction of enterprise AI agents. Microsoft Foundry, model endpoints, application runtimes, retrieval systems, enterprise APIs, and orchestration components can be combined to create agent-driven applications. Understanding these systems requires more than learning how to write prompts. Engineers must understand the relationship between model reasoning, application control flow, tool execution, persistent state, memory, and distributed agent coordination. AI Agents.content: IT Brief Asia - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief Asia logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.asia) ![NiCE launches Cognigy update with AI agent governance](https://itbrief.asia/uploads/story/2026/11/16/business-dashboard-ai-customer-service-agents-office-story-324546.webp) [CX](https://itbrief.asia/tag/customer-experience) [ERP](https://itbrief.asia/tag/enterprise-resource-planning) [LLMs](https://itbrief.asia/tag/large-language-models) # NiCE launches Cognigy update with AI agent governance Mon, 16th Nov 2026 (Today) [![Mara Sugue](https://itbrief.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTg1OSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--c35d782a2ad379dbb3ebd1d7a0269b918cf68f7f/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/maraheadshot.webp) MARA SUGUE News Editor](/author/mara-sugue) NiCE has launched the next generation of NiCE Cognigy, adding tools to build, trace and govern AI agents. The release comes as consumer-facing AI agents begin appearing in Asia, including Meta's Muse in Singapore and Japan. That is raising new questions for companies about how their systems interact with agents acting on behalf of customers. The updated version of Cognigy is aimed at organisations that want to move beyond single-task automation and manage AI agents across broader customer journeys. It is designed to let teams create skills and personas once, then reuse them across multiple agents. That approach is intended to reduce duplication in development work and give companies a more standardised way to deploy customer service agents at scale. The platform can also connect with external agents, including personal AI agents used by customers, through open standards. **Governance focus** A central part of the release is tracing, which NiCE described as full visibility into each step an AI agent takes. That includes the data and tools the agent uses, along with the decisions it makes. The feature addresses a practical issue for large organisations that want a record of how automated systems behave, particularly when those systems are interacting with customers or other agents. As more businesses test autonomous software in service operations, oversight and auditability have become a larger part of procurement and deployment decisions. The update also introduces AI Assist, which NiCE described as an AI companion that supports setup, testing and improvement across an agent's lifecycle. Another addition is native voice-to-voice support, in which speech-to-speech models process audio end to end. Default speech-to-text, text-to-speech and large language models are included within the conversation price. Premium third-party models from Deepgram, ElevenLabs and Anthropic are also available on a usage basis, while customers can continue using their own model contracts. **Customer interactions** The release reflects a broader market shift as software vendors adapt to the prospect of customer interactions increasingly being handled by software agents rather than only by people. In that environment, a business may need to manage not just its own automated assistants, but also exchanges with third-party agents working for consumers. Meta's rollout of Muse in Singapore, with connectors for services including Grab, Shopee, Singapore Airlines and Agoda, has increased visibility for that possibility in the region. Although the service is not available in Australia, its arrival nearby has sharpened discussion about how local businesses should monitor automated decisions made during digital interactions. Philipp Heltewig, Chief AI Officer, NiCE, said the updated platform was designed for practical deployment rather than experimentation. CASRAI is the reference for research administration — bookmark it for the next question. **On November 12, 2026, artificial intelligence security researchers released a study demonstrating that fast typed decision models deployed in autonomous agent architectures remain critically vulnerable to semantic manipulation through evidence competition.** The experimental framework, titled S1-Evo, reveals that while typed System-1 decision models avoid traditional text-generation hijacking, adversarial context perturbations can systematically flip classification boundaries, bypass safety guardrails, and misroute automated research workflows. ## Adversarial Evidence Competition Bypasses Typed Control Gates In a preprint published on arXiv on November 12, 2026 (arXiv:2611.16937), researchers Kaixiang Wang, Junjie Li, Zhaojiacheng Zhou, Jiong Lou, and Jie Li introduced S1-Evo, a framework engineered to evaluate the security boundaries of typed System-1 ([S1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16937)) decision interfaces. Modern autonomous AI agents increasingly deploy hybrid dual-system architectures: computationally expensive autoregressive Large Language Models (System-2, or S2) handle complex reasoning, while specialized, low-latency S1 models handle routine control flow, input moderation, action authorization, and tool selection. Engineers have widely adopted typed S1 systems—such as TypeSafe AI’s [Jev](https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev), Jared Palmer’s open-weight [Kev](https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev) architecture, and ConvAI Innovations’ [Laya](https://huggingface.co/convaiinnovations/laya) encoder—under the assumption that strict schema output contracts insulate agents from prompt injection attacks. Because S1 models score fixed candidate options, rules, and thresholds in a single forward pass without token-by-token decoding, standard jailbreaks and imperative command overrides typically fail. AI Agents.titleZh: AI agents are becoming identities in their own right, and security needs to catch up - Digital Journal
AI Agents.content: [Skip to content](#wp--skip-link--target) * [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/digitaljournal) * [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/digitaljournal) * [X](https://x.com/digitaljournal) * [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/company/digital-journal/) [![Digital Journal](https://www.digitaljournal.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Digital-Journal-Logo-e1745859786345.png)](https://www.digitaljournal.com/) [Home](https://www.digitaljournal.com/) » [Technology](https://www.digitaljournal.com/hub/technology/) # AI agents are becoming identities in their own right, and security needs to catch up ![Dr. Tim Sandle Avatar](https://www.digitaljournal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/cropped-1725659464210-64x64.jpeg) [Dr. Tim Sandle](https://www.digitaljournal.com/author/tim-sandle/) ![Some in the cybersecurity world see a near future in which artificial intelligence agents fight to defend computer networks from hackers using the same technology to attack](https://www.digitaljournal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/e2c272bbe87510fd7b3adb56b8df266525976092-1.jpg) Some in the cybersecurity world see a near future in which artificial intelligence agents fight to defend computer networks from hackers using the same technology to attack – Copyright AFP Joel Saget The next phase of artificial intelligence is likely to create an unusual identity problem for businesses. Increasingly, the entity attempting to access an online account, purchase a product, change a booking or interrogate a corporate database may not be a person. It may be an AI agent acting for them. This transition from generative to “agentic” AI is important because agents do more than produce content. They can be given objectives, determine intermediate steps and, where permissions allow, perform actions across multiple services. Enterprise products are already moving in this direction, with agents increasingly able to interact with tickets, repositories, messages and other business systems. [Recent developments covered by Digital Journal](https://www.digitaljournal.com/pr/news/access-newswire/cxai-launches-beat-new-agentic-1526029600.html) include systems that can identify outstanding work, prepare the next action and execute approved changes. > This changes the problem from securing AI to securing what AI can *do*. One implication is that businesses may need to distinguish between the customer and the digital agent authorised to represent that customer. Recent [Digital Journal analysis of AI and digital identity](https://www.digitaljournal.com/article/your-next-customer-could-be-an-ai-why-digital-identity-is-heading-for-a-reset/) considered precisely this problem: when an agent books a flight, makes a purchase or changes an insurance policy, the organisation receiving the instruction needs to know not simply who the customer is, but what software is acting for them and what authority has been delegated to it. Dan Moore, Sr. Director of CIAM Strategy & Identity Standards at [FusionAuth](https://fusionauth.io/), expects this to become highly visible to consumers. “Major retailers like Target will have a link on their website asking folks to ‘add Target to your agent’ in the same way they prompt for you to allow notifications or install an app,” he predicts. The comparison is useful. Instead of quietly sharing a username and password with autonomous software, consumers could explicitly establish a service relationship with an agent. That creates the possibility of granting the software narrowly defined permissions which can subsequently be monitored or withdrawn. This is increasingly important because allowing an agent to inherit ordinary human credentials can make it difficult for a service to determine whether an action was initiated by a person or software. Moore predicts there will be a high-profile incident in which “an agent will cause someone to lose a significant amount of money or reputation due to using human credentials directly”. ## Machine speed changes the risk Erin Hamm,...

On November 12, 2026, researchers from Navers Lab, Einsia.AI, and Tsinghua University released Visual Cipher Bench, a rigorous multimodal benchmark assessing long-horizon visual reasoning in autonomous LLM agents across 40 original puzzle tasks without text guidance. Frontier models achieved an overall accuracy of only 26.7% for the leading configuration, exposing a critical capability gap for academic AI laboratories and evaluation researchers relying on text-centric benchmarks. ## Benchmark Architecture: 40 Multi-Step Puzzles and Withheld Text Hints The research team led by Deyao Hong, Jiayi Jiang, Yuchun Chen, Yixuan Shi, and Huan-ang Gao published their findings in [Visual Cipher Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Visual Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16861) (arXiv:2611.16861). The benchmark codebase and dataset are available on [GitHub](https://github.com/Einsia/Visual-Cipher-Bench) and the [Einsia.AI project platform](https://lab.einsia.ai/visual-cipher-bench/). While frontier language-model agents achieve high performance on coding benchmarks like SWE-bench and SWE-Bench Pro, these evaluations rely on explicit text issue descriptions and immediate compiler or test execution feedback. LLMs.content: ![Times Square Chronicles](https://t2conline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Times-Square-Chronicles-sm-masthead.png) ![Times Square Chronicles](https://t2conline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Times-Square-Chronicles-sm-masthead.png) ![Times Square Chronicles](https://t2conline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Times-Square-Chronicles-sm-masthead.png) ## Times Square Chronicles #### Open Source Edge0 Model Brings 145 Billion Parameter AI to a Single Laptop, and Businesses Should Pay Attention ### [Business](https://t2conline.com/category/business/) # Open Source Edge0 Model Brings 145 Billion Parameter AI to a Single Laptop, and Businesses Should Pay Attention ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/9b13a8b619ae1364b5921f3630ee78bbc34fa9a447bcb322686f04fcf5e08a01?s=46&d=blank&r=r) Published on By ![](https://t2conline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Screenshot_20261114_231312.jpg) On November 12, AI developer Edge0 released two large language models, Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B, along with the inference software and deployment tools needed to run them. The company says Edge0-145B is the first open-source model of its size designed to run entirely on a personal computer, with no cloud connection required. The technical claims are specific. The model uses a sparse expert design, so only about 10 billion of its 145 billion parameters are active at any given step. Edge0 reports a peak memory footprint of 29 gigabytes, decoding speeds above 80 tokens per second, typical power draw near 120 watts, and context windows from 128,000 to 256,000 tokens. Compatible hardware includes MacBook Pro laptops with Apple M-series chips and Windows machines with high-end consumer graphics cards. Edge0 also says the model scores competitively with frontier cloud models on coding, reasoning, and agent benchmarks. An important caution: those benchmark results come from Edge0’s own internal testing. Independent evaluations have not yet confirmed them. German outlet KIberblick also noted that while Edge0 calls the release open source, the model ships under a custom license called the Edge0 Community Model License 1.0, so businesses should read the terms before building anything on it. The outlet’s advice for teams is to experiment internally but wait for independent tests before making a decision. **What this means for businesses** **What to do now** Small and mid-sized businesses do not need to rush. A sensible first step is to assign one technical person to test the model on a non-sensitive task and compare the output quality against the cloud tools you already use. Review the license for any restrictions on commercial use. Check whether your current computers meet the memory and graphics requirements, since a 29 gigabyte footprint rules out many standard office machines. The larger takeaway is the direction of travel. Capable AI is moving from rented cloud services toward software businesses can own and run themselves, and companies that start learning how to deploy it locally will be better positioned as that shift continues. It includes diagrams, a small PyTorch implementation, and a survey of 2025 and 2026 open-weight architectures. Sebastian Raschka, PhD, published a technical walkthrough on positional embeddings in large language models on Ahead of AI on Nov. 15, 2026, covering classic methods and RoPE alongside 2026 architecture trends. The article treats position information as a building block for a broader architecture analysis. It assumes readers know basic transformer mechanics and directs readers who need a refresher to Raschka's earlier self-attention walkthrough. ## Where position information enters an LLM A tokenizer turns text into token IDs. An embedding layer maps each ID to a vector. Transformer blocks update those vectors through attention and feed-forward layers. An output layer produces next-token logits. GPT-2 adds position vectors to token embeddings before the first transformer block. MiniMax-M3 injects position information inside attention with RoPE. The figure highlights token embedding layers in both models. ## Why order changes meaning Swapping "red" and "gray" in "The red fox jumps over the gray fox" changes which fox jumps. Both occurrences of "fox" receive token ID 2, so the embedding layer returns the same vector for each. Without position information, attention scores between token pairs stay the same when words move. A causal mask supplies some order information. In an autoregressive model, "jumps" can attend to "red" in the first sentence and "gray" in the second. The mask does not encode distance: it cannot distinguish a gap of one token from a gap of ten tokens. Explicit positional methods supply that distance. ## GPT-2: learned absolute embeddings GPT-2 adds a learned position vector to each token embedding before the first transformer block. The token embedding and position embedding layers share dimensions, so their vectors add element by element. Raschka shows the GPT-2 XL dimensions and a PyTorch module excerpt. GPT-2 stores 1,024 position vectors. That fixed table sets the context length before training. Extending the table later costs money and compute because the table grows with context length. In GPT-2 Medium, the position table accounts for 0.30% of model weights at 1,024 positions. At a 100,000-token context, it would account for more than 22%. GPT-2 did not need the transformer's scaling because its token embeddings started with a standard deviation of 0.02 and its position embeddings with 0.01. This is an absolute method: the vector for a token depends on its index from the start of the sequence. The two "fox" tokens start with the same embedding, but position vectors at indices 2 and 7 make their inputs differ before attention. ## The 2017 transformer: fixed sinusoidal encodings The original transformer paper from 2017 uses the same addition mechanism with fixed sine and cosine functions. The model scales token embeddings by the square root of the embedding width before adding position vectors. Raschka attributes that scaling to keeping token and position values on comparable numerical scales at initialization. Each position vector contains sine and cosine pairs. Written and maintained by[CASRAI Editorial Board](/about/editorial-policy) Published * [X](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcasrai.org%2Fguides%2Fmetr-time-horizon&text=METR%20Time%20Horizon%3A%20AI%20Evaluation%20Framework%20and%20Capability%20Benchmarks&via=YourCASRAI "Share on X") * [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcasrai.org%2Fguides%2Fmetr-time-horizon "Share on LinkedIn") * [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fcasrai.org%2Fguides%2Fmetr-time-horizon "Share on Facebook") On this page The METR time horizon is an empirical AI evaluation metric that quantifies the autonomous capability of frontier artificial intelligence models by measuring the length of complex tasks—expressed in human expert completion time—that an AI agent can execute independently with a specified reliability threshold, typically 50% or 80%. Originally established in 2022 as ARC Evals under Paul Christiano’s Alignment Research Center, the team spun out as an independent non-profit entity in 2023 under the executive leadership of Beth Barnes. METR’s core mandate centers on empirical capability testing, pre-deployment risk assessment, and technical red-teaming for leading AI developers, national safety institutes, and scientific oversight bodies, as detailed in our guide to [What Is METR?](/guides/what-is-metr). Traditional language model benchmarks, such as MMLU or HumanEval, suffer from rapid ceiling saturation and measure isolated knowledge retrieval rather than sustained, multi-turn agency. METR introduced the task-completion time horizon to solve this measurement challenge by mapping model success rates against the duration of labor a human specialist requires to finish the identical assignment. On November 14, 2026, researchers from Stanford University’s SNAP group, in collaboration with computer scientists from MIT, the University of Pennsylvania, and the University of Toronto, open-sourced Memorilla, an architecture that provides frozen large language models with persistent, query-conditioned access to extensive document collections. By translating document corpora into compact latent vectors rather than packing raw text into prompts, Memorilla compresses context by over a hundredfold while preserving critical facts and inter-document relationships across long-horizon research and agent workflows. ## Open-Source Release and Core Technical Architecture The Memorilla system, published under the permissive Apache 2.0 license, was developed by doctoral researchers Adibvafa Fallahpour, Parsa Idehpour, Vignesh Kothapalli, Nikita Mounier, Shirley Wu, and Shayan Pardis alongside Professor Jure Leskovec at the Stanford Network Analysis Project (SNAP). The codebase is hosted on GitHub at <https://github.com/snap-stanford/memorilla>, with pre-trained checkpoints on Hugging Face at <https://huggingface.co/memorilla> and interactive documentation at <https://memory.stanford.edu/>. Theoretical foundations and benchmark validations appear in the preprint *Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs* on arXiv ([arXiv:2610.21375](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21375)). Rather than requiring model parameter fine-tuning or expanding active context windows, Memorilla acts as a modular bridge connecting frozen document encoders to frozen text decoders. The framework meets established [open-source model criteria](/dictionary/term/open-source-model-criteria), distributing complete training recipes, attention profiling harnesses, and evaluation suites. AI Product.content: [![](https://assets.bizclikmedia.net/original/5401dac120314d7e0f03205da6e95493:6da76f0b8571199734ddc929a0b434ce/technology-magazine-light-logo.png)](/ "Home") Article AI & Machine Learning # Asana’s CPO on why workflow readiness beats AI model hype By[Alice Chambers](/author/alice-chambers) November 15, 2026 undefined mins Share this article **Prioritise Us** on Google Share this article **Prioritise Us** on Google ![](https://assets.bizclikmedia.net/138/791a25a17528cda49d3c3849bd6fbfcd:d906b26b7f217c9f6783576bd3265f53/arnab-bose.webp) “AI can produce useful output and complete individual tasks, but enterprises need more,” Arnab says Arnab Bose, Chief Product Officer at Asana, reveals how StackAI’s integration and shared operating layers help enterprises scale AI agents safely Since joining [Asana](https://technologymagazine.com/company/asana) as Chief Product Officer in September 2025 – following a six-year tenure at Okta – [Arnab Bose](https://technologymagazine.com/executive/arnab-bose) has led the company’s product strategy, focusing on how enterprises coordinate complex work across human and AI teams. In this Q&A, Arnab explores why organisations struggle to move artificial intelligence beyond isolated pilots into scaled, high-impact operations. He discusses closing the human-agent coordination gap, the importance of “workflow readiness”, and how a shared operating layer bolstered by Asana’s acquisition of StackAI – provides essential context, governance and accountability to embed AI directly where enterprise work already happens. ## A year into your role – what’s the problem you’re now more convinced than ever nobody has solved yet? The hardest problem an organisation continues to face isn’t whether an AI agent can perform a certain task, we know it can. Instead, the biggest challenge is closing the coordination gap between humans and agents. AI can produce useful output and complete individual tasks, but enterprises need more. Truly collaborative work involves shared goals, dependencies, decisions, approvals and handoffs, factors often beyond isolated AI agents’ capabilities. To bridge this gap, agents need access to the right context for a task; that context turns AI from generic output into meaningful value. Currently, many AI experiences still operate around one person, one prompt and one agent, essentially operating in a ‘black box’. This single player approach leads to work that lacks crucial context and therefore often misses the mark. According to recent Asana research, only 18% of UK workers say AI agents meet their needs, while 33% say they address some important needs, revealing significant gaps in AI utility. Bridging these gaps and scaling AI to become truly impactful remains a key challenge. For me, the remaining problem is embedding AI agents within existing workflows and giving them a shared system of context, memory and coordination. ## What does the gap between a successful pilot and a scaled workflow actually look like? Pilots are an important starting point, but they are also often where organisations get stuck. Pilots tend to operate in a narrow environment with isolated information and under close human supervision. This often means pilots succeed within their limited parameters and under close human management; the challenge comes when they scale across an organisation, where those strict parameters become huge ecosystems. A scaled workflow, by contrast, has AI agents operating with organisation-wide intelligence informing their work at all times. Pilots often stall at scale because context is lost across applications, tools and software; handoffs become invisible; and ownership becomes unclear. To scale a successful pilot, embed AI where work already happens, rather than treating AI tools as an add-on. A successful pilot may demonstrate that an AI agent can complete a task. Advertisement ## Adobe Investment Narrative Recap To own Adobe, you need to believe its creative and experience software can stay embedded in professional workflows even as AI reshapes how content is produced. According to HarishPK, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, the core thesis rests on durable cash generation and a wide moat around industry standard tools rather than short bursts of hypergrowth. The key near term catalyst is whether AI driven features and credit usage translate into steadier revenue and earnings delivery, given forecasts for mid single digit growth and a P/E near 13x. The biggest risk is that generative AI compresses pricing power or accelerates churn, and the latest announcements do not materially change that risk yet but show active product execution. The expanded Adobe partnership with Google is the clearest operational bridge between the AI story and near term catalysts. Embedding Acrobat into Workspace and bringing Adobe tools into Gemini and AI Mode in Search positions Adobe closer to where users already spend their time. This could support engagement and usage intensity if execution stays tight. At the same time, opening Adobe Firefly and Creative Cloud to Google’s imaging and video models, plus Gemini inside Acrobat, raises both opportunity and complexity. It strengthens distribution and keeps Adobe in the AI conversation, yet also increases reliance on partners and puts more focus on how quickly Adobe can ship reliable, on brand AI workflows that justify its current pricing and HarishPK’s moat driven thesis. Based on HarishPK’s narrative, the fair value of Adobe is US$319.96 per share, using revenue growth of 8.9% a year and a future profit margin of 29.5%. These assumptions underpin a cash flow driven view of what the current AI and moat story could justify over time. On November 14, 2026, researchers from Stanford University’s SNAP group, in collaboration with computer scientists from MIT, the University of Pennsylvania, and the University of Toronto, open-sourced Memorilla, an architecture that provides frozen large language models with persistent, query-conditioned access to extensive document collections. By translating document corpora into compact latent vectors rather than packing raw text into prompts, Memorilla compresses context by over a hundredfold while preserving critical facts and inter-document relationships across long-horizon research and agent workflows. ## Open-Source Release and Core Technical Architecture The Memorilla system, published under the permissive Apache 2.0 license, was developed by doctoral researchers Adibvafa Fallahpour, Parsa Idehpour, Vignesh Kothapalli, Nikita Mounier, Shirley Wu, and Shayan Pardis alongside Professor Jure Leskovec at the Stanford Network Analysis Project (SNAP). The codebase is hosted on GitHub at <https://github.com/snap-stanford/memorilla>, with pre-trained checkpoints on Hugging Face at <https://huggingface.co/memorilla> and interactive documentation at <https://memory.stanford.edu/>. Theoretical foundations and benchmark validations appear in the preprint *Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs* on arXiv ([arXiv:2610.21375](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21375)). Rather than requiring model parameter fine-tuning or expanding active context windows, Memorilla acts as a modular bridge connecting frozen document encoders to frozen text decoders. [Getting informed](https://www.cointribune.com/en/tag/getting-informed-en/) ▪ [Artificial Intelligence](https://www.cointribune.com/en/tag/artificial-intelligence-en/) Summarize this article with: Qubic’s scientific team does not hand-design the brains of its Neuraxon agents: it lets evolution search for them. For ARC-AGI-3, the interactive benchmark of the ARC Prize 2026, the team tested more than 110 configurations and millions of evolved brains on about 500 CPU cores, with no GPU and no pretrained model, according to Neuraxon Intelligence Academy Vol. 14. Its best offline score reached 0.38, and its latest Kaggle submission scored 0.41. This guide explains how evolutionary neural architecture search works, how Neuraxon brains play ARC-AGI-3, what the experiments revealed, what Neuraxon 3.0 will search for next, and how to download the code and the 603,054-row dataset behind it. [Read us on Google News](https://news.google.com/publications/CAAqBwgKMOedqAsw1KjAAw?hl=en-US&gl=US&ceid=US%3Aen) ## In Brief * Neural architecture search (NAS) automates the design of a network’s structure, not just the tuning of its weights. * Neuraxon uses evolutionary search: brains inherit parameters, mutate, and the best ones reproduce. * On ARC-AGI-3, the team evolved millions of brains on about 500 CPU cores with no GPU; its latest Kaggle submission scored 0.41, up from 0.38. * The experiments exposed the winner’s curse: brains that cleared a game on every seed used to select them failed on new seeds. * Neuraxon 3.0 will select brains on how fast they learn in games they have never seen, under a protocol fixed before any data is collected. * The code is open source (MIT for the core) and the evolved brains are published on Hugging Face (82.7 GB). ## What Is Neural Architecture Search? Neural architecture search is the automated design of a neural network’s structure: how many units it has, how they connect, and which rules update them. Training adjusts the strength of connections inside a fixed design; NAS decides the design itself. The field’s reference survey, by [Elsken, Metzen and Hutter (JMLR, 2019)](https://jmlr.org/papers/v20/18-598.html), breaks every NAS method into three parts. 1. **A search space:** the set of architectures the method is allowed to consider. 2. **A search strategy:** the way it explores that space. 3. **A performance estimate:** the way it decides which candidate is better, without fully training every one. Think of it as the difference between learning to cook and designing the kitchen. Training teaches a network to cook well; NAS decides where the oven, the sink and the worktop go. ### Four strategies, four cost profiles Four families of search strategies dominate the literature, as summarized in [our introduction to neural architecture search](https://qubic.org/blog-detail/neural-architecture-search-who-designs-the-brain-neuraxon-intelligence-academy-vol-14). CASRAI is the reference for research administration — bookmark it for the next question. **On November 12, 2026, researchers released a comprehensive study detailing a four-level failure taxonomy for live streaming dictation automatic speech recognition (ASR), demonstrating that standard word error rate (WER) metrics systematically conceal severe transcription failures.** Published as an arXiv preprint by speech researchers at heylemon.ai, the benchmark streamed identical speech across eleven production models, finding that systems with near-identical overall WER diverge dramatically under whispering, acoustic background noise, and multilingual code-switching. In streaming dictation, speech recognition operates under distinct constraints compared to offline transcription. When users dictate messages, notes, or research logs, audio streams continuously and text inserts directly into applications. While conventional benchmarks evaluate pre-recorded files after stripping punctuation, capitalization, and numbers, live dictation requires users to manually detect and correct every omitted or misplaced word. ## What the benchmark uncovered across eleven ASR systems The study, titled “Beyond Word Error Rate: A Failure Taxonomy of Streaming Dictation ASR” ([arXiv:2611.16919](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16919)), was conducted by Harras Mansoor, Muhammad Wisal, Hassan Bhatti, and Masood Shakir. The team evaluated eleven real-time speech systems: two self-hosted open models (Qwen3-ASR 1.7B and Whisper Large V3) alongside nine provider-hosted streaming services, including Meta Muse Voice Transcribe, Google Gemini 3.5 Transcribe (Live API), Deepgram Nova-3, AssemblyAI Universal-3.6 Pro and Universal-3.5 Pro, Zoom Scribe, ElevenLabs, OpenAI GPT-Live-Transcribe, and OpenAI Realtime Whisper. The primary dataset comprised 106 scripted English dictations from a single speaker under three acoustic conditions: a quiet room, with a fan on, and whispered speech. Holding speaker acoustics constant enabled rigorous cross-model isolation. Open Source AI.content: [Skip to content](#wp--skip-link--target) # Obscurify.ai Implements Unlinkable Inference and Blind Signatures for Private AI Access Distributed by EIN Presswire • 5 min read * [Technology](/press-release/?topic=technology) *The anonymous AI chat now pays for each conversation with blind-signed digital cash, so it can’t tell whose chat it is or which chats belong together.* WASHINGTON, DC, UNITED STATES, November 15, 2026 /[EINPresswire.com](https://www.einpresswire.com/)/ — AI chat service [Obscurify.ai](https://obscurify.ai/?utm_source=einpresswire) released an [open source library](https://github.com/Obscurify-ai/unlinkable-inference) today that enables AI services to offer “[unlinkable inference](https://obscurify.ai/blog/unlinkable_inference?utm_source=einpresswire)”, where the service cannot tell whose conversation it is processing or which conversations are from the same user. The Obscurify.ai web chat and Android app now use this technique. The term “unlinkable inference” was coined by the Open Anonymity Project, which uses a similar approach in its anonymous chat app, OA. Most AI services (including many that claim to be “private”) attach an account key to every request that you make. So even without a name or email address, the provider can link all of your conversations together. One slip in any conversation can identify all the rest. Users have a wallet of digital vouchers in their app, which have been “signed” (but not seen) by Obscurify.ai using a technique called “blind signatures” (described by cryptographer David Chaum in 1982 and standardized by the IETF in 2023 as RFC 9474). Each time you start a new conversation, the app creates a “prepaid session” which is paid for with a handful of these vouchers and identified only by a random secret. After a period of inactivity, the session is closed and the remaining balance is returned to you as new vouchers (which the service has never seen). The service can verify that the vouchers are genuine but it can’t tell which account they came from or link conversations together. “An account number (no email address required) was a good start, but every chat still had that same account key attached to it,” said a spokesperson for Obscurify.ai. “Unlinkable inference removes the account key from the conversation. We can validate that someone paid for it, but we cannot link conversations together or to an identity.” Two things are notable about this design. First, each chat session’s unused balance is refunded to your device as new blind vouchers. Second, your entire wallet can be restored from your account number. And it doesn’t cost you anything extra. Each conversation is billed for the exact number of tokens it uses (to the thousandth of a cent) and nothing in an open session is ever lost. Since every voucher is derived from your 16-digit account number, you’ll recover your wallet the next time you sign in (even if your phone is factory reset or you close your Tor Browser window). Subscribers will have their plan’s models available via anonymous monthly “passes” which only indicate the plan tier. According to its documentation, the service can read the prompts you send to AI models and can see your IP address if you don’t use Tor or a virtual private network. So if you write a prompt that identifies you, it will still be able to identify you. Open source for any service The open source release is built around a Rust library: unlinkable-inference (MIT and Apache 2.0 licensed). A WebAssembly build for web pages is on npm. The “unlinkability” is implemented on both the client and server side in this library, which means that an AI company can install it on their own servers and database, without the need for a “broker” or other third party. There’s also a command-line proxy (GPL licensed) that works with coding agents (and anything else that uses the OpenAI or Anthropic API) – those tools will get private sessions with no changes. On November 12, 2026, researchers at the Wharton Generative AI Labs released **Primer**, an open-source, model-agnostic AI framework that enables educators to author customized, voice-enabled educational simulations directly from lesson plans and rubrics. By pairing an instructor-in-the-loop authoring pipeline with a three-tier runtime system, Primer offers academic institutions a transparent blueprint for deploying adaptive simulations while preserving teacher intent and student data governance. ## Wharton Generative AI Labs Releases Primer On November 12, 2026, an interdisciplinary team from the Wharton Generative AI Labs at the University of Pennsylvania—Ethan Mollick, Lilach Mollick, Ben Przystanski, LJ Ciccarelli, Natalie Bach, and Laura Zarrow—published the preprint *Primer: An AI Framework for Instructor-Centered Educational Simulation Creation* ([arXiv:2611.16986](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16986)). Alongside the research paper, the team published the complete open-source codebase, prompt templates, and runtime architecture on GitHub ([wharton-generative-ai-labs/primer](https://github.com/wharton-generative-ai-labs/primer)). The initiative was supported by philanthropic funding from the Bezos Family Foundation, the Walton Family Foundation, and Charles and Lynn Schusterman Family Philanthropies. Educational simulations have long been recognized as high-impact pedagogical tools for professional training, clinical practice, negotiation, and scientific inquiry. By immersing learners in contextual challenges where decisions carry visible consequences, simulations bridge theoretical knowledge and practical execution. However, traditional simulation development has historically presented an insurmountable barrier for most instructors: building realistic scenarios, developing consistent character interactions, scripting scaffolding, and engineering interactive branching logic typically demands specialized software development teams, instructional design consultants, and substantial financial budgets. Infra & Chips.titleZh: Central Asia's AI Race: Big Ambitions, Even Bigger Risks
Infra & Chips.content: Central Asian governments are rushing to join the global AI race. And they're going big. NVIDIA has partnered with US infrastructure firm Firebird and Kazakhtelecom on Data Center Valley, a project in Kazakhstan billed as Central Asia’s largest AI infrastructure development. Uzbekistan is pursuing similar ambitions under its Digital Uzbekistan 2030 strategy, offering tax and customs exemptions through 2040 for qualifying data-center investments. And Tajikistan announced plans in October for a regional AI innovation hub supported by US chipmaker Nvidia’s Global AI Nations program. Critics of Central Asia’s AI ambitions, however, have flagged shaky financing, reliance on coal-fired power in countries already facing electricity shortfalls, and a lack of transparency in a region long plagued by corruption. ## **Data Center Valley** With an announced price tag of $10 billion for its initial rollout, backers of Data Center Valley say it will turn Kazakhstan into a major exporter of AI computing power. When then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang visited Astana in October, he said the initial expansion of the project could eventually reach 1 gigawatt (GW) of power capacity for servers and equipment, with longer-term ambitions of up to 5 GW. During a televised conversation with Kazakh Deputy Prime Minister and Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Minister Zhaslan Madiyev, Huang presented the country as ideally placed to become a major player in the global AI industry. “While the rest of the world is deciding how to engage and how to build an AI economy, here in Kazakhstan, you are doing it already," Huang said. "Kazakhstan has a fundamental advantage because you have so much natural resources already and you have so much energy. Instead of just exporting energy in the future, you could transform the energy into intelligence and export intelligence." Your browser doesn’t support HTML5 Marat Beksultanov, a New York-based geospatial analyst and CEO of GeoBox, a satellite analytics and remote-sensing company specializing in water management and precision agriculture in Central Asia, questioned the finances behind Data Center Valley. “The biggest pitfall is that it's majority-financed by the Kazakh government," Beksultanov said. "There's very little, if any, private money that goes into this. And it's financing and funding this project before anybody committed to using it. And that's the other side of it. So, there's very little that we know of in terms of who will be the ultimate customer for this particular project." In Kazakhstan, Huang said that the country could turn its energy resources into computing power and export it to European markets. The Data Center Valley project is close to the coal-fired Ekibastuz GRES-1 power plant. But Beksultanov said that could be a problem. “European companies are the customers least willing to buy dirty power. Many of them must report the carbon footprint of the services they buy, including cloud computing. A data center running on Ekibastuz coal adds to that footprint. To sell to Europe, the project needs clean power it does not have,” the GeoBox CEO said. Whether Kazakhstan produces enough electricity to run large data centers is also unclear. “Kazakhstan does not produce enough electricity for itself today. NVIDIA has partnered with US infrastructure firm Firebird and Kazakhtelecom on Data Center Valley, a project in Kazakhstan billed as Central Asia’s largest AI infrastructure development.
